Let me preface this by saying I don't pirate myself and don't advocate it, but for sake of attempting an answer: piracy adds market pressure where there might otherwise be very little. Cable TV, for example. One provider can secure the distribution rights to whatever exclusives they want, and you have to go to them to get the content. They can get away with more predatory pricing and practices because they're the only one holding the content you're interested in. Their only competition in this case is "going without". Add piracy into the mix and suddenly they're competing with those who, given enough motivation, can obtain the content through less than optimal means. Now the content provider has a greater incentive to offer fair and easy access to their content instead of locking things up behind inflated prices or a bunch of inconvenient hurdles.

Piracy has its own unique role in cultural development. Early film cameras saw a lot of development by people who snuck back to their home countries to dodge patent issues and then improve upon the designs. Pirate radio played things that normally would not or could not get played. The mp3 moved the world away from the old model of paying $15 for a CD with only one or two enjoyable songs on it to people carrying storage devices filled with their own personalized radio stations. A lot of people who admit to piracy often say that through pirating they discovered artists they would never have known about otherwise, which in turn lead them to supporting the newfound artists they loved buy paying for their content.

If you're willing to read a whole book on the subject, consider picking up The Pirate's Dilemma by Matt Mason.

There are a lot of good arguments in this thread, but I'll add mine here. First, piracy is a response to market conditions and evolving technology. It is pretty much saying "I don't like how [Media Company] is providing their content, so I'm going to go elsewhere." It is competition and a free market at its purest; pirate copies are the direct response to Old Media's failure to capitalize on the internet and the free distribution systems that it provides.

This is also why companies that get it have flourished. Spotify, for $5 a month ($10 for non-students), provides me the ability to pull up pretty much any song at will and listen to it or add it to my playlists. What I get from Spotify isn't music, it's convenience and integration among all my devices. With Pandora, I get music discovery based on what I already listen to. Same with Steam: I don't get games, I get easy updates, cloud-based saves, multiplayer and social features, and easy availability (being able to click a game in my library and install it rather than having to hoard installers and cracks). I can get everything I buy on these services for free through piracy, but I pay for them (Steam and Spotify directly, Pandora through advertising) since they provide something beyond what piracy provides. Piracy created and exemplified the market for digital media and these companies capitalized on it.

Unfortunately, there isn't a good single solution for movies/tv shows like other media. Shows and films are split among three major services (Netflix, Hulu, and Amazon Prime) and even with all three there are plenty of things that still aren't available at all (I had to pirate The Flash (1990) for example). As a result, I simply pirate what I want to watch if it isn't available on one of the three services I have access to and if it wasn't for mooching of off family members' accounts, I'd probably not bother with legal alternatives since they really don't provide anything that pirating doesn't (and in many cases are more limited than simply using Project Free TV or other sites). Piracy is a service and availability problem, and competing with it by providing something better is necessary in this day and age if you don't want people to simply go out and pirate your shit.

Second, as an angle that isn't considered often, pirates are archivists and some of the best at it in the world. They are extraordinarily efficient at it due to having a passion for whatever they're archiving and sharing, make no money from it (often spending a lot money to get better sources), and preserve culture better than any library could.

Take for example the Stellaview, a forgotten accessory for the Super Famicom. [Archive] There are pirate enthusiasts working tirelessly to preserve the Stellaview lineup, and if it wasn't for them most of these games would have been lost to time completely. As it stands now, some have been lost completely despite their best efforts.

Likewise, when I decided to take a little nostalgia trip a few months ago by watching Bear in the Big Blue House, I discovered only around 35 of the show's ~120 episodes were released on US DVD, but I was able to find around 55 episodes through piracy, including the officially released episodes. Some were shitty cams, some VHS or TV Rips, and none were DVD quality. I since have made it a little project to get what DVDs I can, whether import or US, and rip them in good quality to my Hard Drive so I know they exist somewhere, including so far 3 episodes I couldn't find at all and another that was incomplete. I do it because I love the show and think that it should continue to exist despite the attempt at pushing the show down the memory hole.

By doing what libraries have been doing for more than a century, pirates preserve and share culture in a vastly more efficient manner than any library bound by corrupt copyright law and/or physical limitation ever could.
